name: PT Asiaplast Industries Tbk

frontmatter.title: Asiaplast Industries - the base case is in the price and the remedy is the option
frontmatter.summary: The fire is behind Asiaplast and the nine-month accounts show the recovery is real, but our target is Rp255 against a Rp258 price, so the base case is already in the market. What the price does not pay for is the option on a full remedy, which we weight at 25% and which the house illiquidity discount largely removes. We rate the shares HOLD [S0, S2].
thesis: The trough is past and it is in the numbers, not in a forecast. Nine-month revenue was IDR247.3bn and gross profit IDR40.9bn, the replacement calender runs from the fourth quarter, and our FY2026E revenue of IDR347.9bn requires the quarter to run about fifteen per cent above the third quarter, which the restarted calender makes possible [S7, S2, F23, F30, F31].

The balance sheet carries a claim the data pack omits. The IDR41.1bn controller loan pays no interest, has no term and is unchanged at 30 September 2026; we deduct it at face and carry the risk of a call in the bear case [S2, S7, F12, F13, F37].

The DCF is the target, not a blend. The DCF gives Rp226 a share and the probability tree and the illiquidity discount bring that to Rp255, within a percent of the price; the trailing multiples are not published because they are struck on the fire year [S0].

The remedy is the option the price does not pay for. A calender at nameplate, an import measure and a lower cost of capital take the bull to Rp726 on a 25% weight, against Rp44 in a genuine down cycle [S0, S4, S5].

The base rate is why the bull is not weighted higher, because capex turnarounds in this market work less than half the time and this one still needs a policy decision that has not been made [S0, S2, F17, F18].

blocks.text: Asiaplast Industries is a small Indonesian plastics converter with an electronics sideline. It buys petrochemical resin, sheet and film, converts them into plastics for industrial customers, and owns 35,000 MT of installed plastics capacity at Tangerang, of which 5,400 MT of polypropylene and high-impact polystyrene sheet was added in 2025 and is still very lightly used [S2, F6, F26, F27]. In October 2024 a calender in the Flexible Film and Sheet business burned, and because the replacement was ordered late it only runs after mid-2026; plastics production in FY2025 was 10,970 MT, a utilisation rate of 31.3% of installed capacity, and revenue fell 24.8% that year [S2, F5, F7, F20, F23]. The reported FY2025 net profit of IDR5.6bn was largely an insurance effect: other income was IDR11.9bn, of which IDR8.7bn was the fire claim, while the operating line excluding it was negative, at IDR-6.2bn [S2, F15, F16].

The recovery is no longer a forecast. Revenue for the nine months to 30 September 2026 was IDR247.3bn, gross profit was IDR40.9bn, reported operating profit was IDR11.8bn of which IDR3.9bn was other income, and net profit to owners of the parent was IDR7.5bn [S7, F30, F31, F32, F33, F38]. That is a business earning a gross margin a shade under seventeen per cent and a clean operating margin in the middle single digits, which is a recovery from the fire but not a return to the margins of the last undisrupted year [S7, S2].

Our conclusion is that this is now fairly valued. The DCF, struck on a through-cycle Brent price and a cost of capital built from the rupiah risk-free rate, gives Rp226 a share [S0]. The probability tree gives a weighted Rp318, and after the house illiquidity discount of 20% for a stock that trades about IDR106.7m a day the target is Rp255, -0.4% from the last price [S0]. We rate the shares HOLD [S0].

Three things move the value. The first is volume through the replacement calender: the capacity is paid for, and the distance between 35,000 MT of nameplate and 10,970 MT of trough production is the whole operating-leverage story, tempered by the fact that 5,400 MT of it is a new line the company concedes is barely used [S2, F5, F6, F26, F27]. The second is the resin spread: raw materials are IDR186.0bn of IDR264.9bn of cost of goods sold, so the Brent deck matters, and the deck has Brent at US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E against US$68.1/bbl in FY2025A before it falls back to US$75.0/bbl [S0, F10]. The third is the balance sheet, which has just distributed a large part of its cash to the controlling family that owns most of the shares and carries a related-party claim the data pack does not show [S2, S3, F12, F22].

Asiaplast is a converter, not a petrochemical producer. It buys polymer resin from domestic and imported suppliers, extrudes and laminates it into film, sheet and rigid packaging, and sells the output to industrial and consumer-goods customers. Converting is a spread business: the margin is the difference between the resin price and the price the customer will pay for the finished article, minus the cost of running the plant. Because resin is a globally traded commodity priced off oil, the industry's cost base moves with crude, and because the finished article is bulky, low-value and easy to ship, import competition is permanent and pricing power is limited to service, lead time and specification. The economics therefore turn on utilisation and on how much of a resin move can be recovered in price. A plant running at a third of capacity still carries the same fixed overhead, which is why the margin at the trough of a volume cycle is not representative of the margin at normal running rates.

Asiaplast Industries runs two reportable segments. Plastics is the business that matters: it converts polypropylene, polyethylene and PET into flexible film and sheet, rigid sheet and packaging, and polypropylene sheet, and it generated IDR293.0bn of the IDR300.5bn of FY2025 revenue [S2, F8]. Electronics generated IDR7.4bn and lost money at the operating line, and the company has said it will work with other firms to sell air-conditioning units, repairs and cleaning rather than run the segment as it did before [S2, F9]. The segment table shows the plastics business earning an operating profit while electronics lost money [S2].

The manufacturing base is a single site in Tangerang with 35,000 MT of installed plastics capacity and 147 employees at the last count [S0, S2, F6]. That nameplate is not one homogeneous plant: 5,400 MT of polypropylene and high-impact polystyrene sheet capacity was added in 2025, and the annual report says the utilisation of the new machines is still very low, especially the polypropylene sheet line [S2, F26, F27]. We therefore treat the productive base the forecast has to fill as the nameplate less that new line, about twenty-nine and a half thousand tonnes, rather than the full nameplate [S0, S2, F6, F26, F27].

Production in FY2025 was 10,970 MT, a utilisation rate of 31.3%, and the annual report attributes that directly to the calender that burned in October 2024 and to the delay in buying its replacement [S2, F5, F6, F7]. The board's own account is that the new machine will only run after mid-2026, and the nine-month accounts show the first part of the recovery: revenue is running about twelve per cent ahead of the comparable period and the gross margin has recovered to the high teens [S7, S2, F23]. That is the single most important operating fact about this company today: it owns a plant with roughly three times the capacity it was using in the trough year, and the first tranche of that capacity is now being used.

The strategy has three strands. The first is to fill the reinstalled capacity, which the annual report argues is possible because unused capacity is available [S2]. The second is downstream diversification into polypropylene sheet, the 2025 investment which has not yet earned its capital [S2, F26]. The third is to stop losing money in electronics, which it is scaling down and re-scoping toward services [S2, F9]. We treat the first as credible because the capacity exists and the machine is a like-for-like replacement; we treat the second as a caution rather than an asset, because it is the most recent evidence on how this management team allocates capital.

Customers are spread. No single customer accounted for more than a tenth of revenue in FY2025 or FY2024, and the company discloses that explicitly [S2, F25]. That is a genuine strength relative to the size of the segment because it removes the risk of a single buyer walking, but it also means the company has no anchor customer to fill a new machine and must win volume in a market the industry association describes as flooded with imports [S2, S4, S5, F25]. Revenue is domestic in the main; the annual report describes an industrial customer base and the geographic note discloses no material export concentration [S2].

Ownership is the defining structural fact. The controlling shareholder holds the company through a family structure: PT Maco Amangraha holds the controlling block, the President Commissioner holds the next largest stake, the public, meaning holders below five per cent, accounts for 12.7%, and the ultimate beneficiary also serves as President Commissioner while his wife and sons sit in the ownership chain [S2, F22]. We deal with the consequences in section six; for the business description the point is that this is a family-controlled converter in which the free float is small enough that the share price is a residual of family decisions rather than of institutional flows [S0, S2, F22].

The Indonesian plastics converting industry is in a documented squeeze. The industry association, INAPLAS, told the industry ministry in November 2026 that domestic plastics plants are running at only sixty to seventy per cent of capacity because imported plastic is being sold at dumping prices, and asked for safeguard and anti-dumping measures [S4, S5]. The same account says that if imports were curbed the industry could push utilisation to eighty or ninety per cent [S5]. The minister's response was sympathetic in principle: he said the ministry would protect domestic industry by every means available, naming the national standards regime and anti-dumping among them, but no measure has been imposed and none has a timetable [S6]. This is the operating environment in which Asiaplast must fill a machine that would take it to roughly three times its trough volume.

The cost side is oil. The company's raw materials are petrochemical, and the deck has Brent at US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E against US$68.1/bbl in FY2025A, before it falls to US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E, US$78.0/bbl in FY2029E and the long-run US$75.0/bbl [S0, F10]. For a converter a resin spike is a working-capital and a margin event at the same time: the inventory has to be financed at the higher price and the customer resists the increase. We model an eighty-five per cent pass-through of a cost link that covers seventy per cent of cost of goods sold, which leaves about a tenth of cost exposed to the oil move, and that is what produces the margin dip we forecast for FY2026E even as volumes recover [S0, S2, F10].

The rupiah is the second external variable. The firm brief puts the macro regime in balance-of-payments pressure with the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD against a spot of Rp18,004/USD, and the central bank rate at 5.8% [S0]. Asiaplast's exposure is indirect but real: imported resin and imported competing finished goods are both dollar-priced, so a weaker rupiah raises the cost of resin and simultaneously makes imported plastic more expensive for Indonesian buyers, which is the one channel through which a weak currency helps a domestic converter [S2]. The company also discloses dollar-denominated monetary liabilities in its currency note, so the direct translation exposure is measured rather than open-ended [S2].

Competitive position is that of a sub-scale challenger. The installed base of 35,000 MT is small in national terms, and the company competes against importers who, on the association's account, can land product more cheaply than domestic plants can make it [S2, S4, S5, F6]. Its advantages are specification and service, because a converter that can hold tolerances and deliver on time earns a place on a customer's approved list, and the absence of customer concentration suggests it has several such places [S2, F25]. Its disadvantages are cost and scale. There is no evidence of pricing power in the record: the gross margin has ranged from 20.7% to 24.9% and back to 11.8% over four years, and the swing tracks volume and resin rather than any stable premium [S2, S0].

The five-forces picture is unattractive. Supplier power sits with the resin producers, who price off a global benchmark that a converter of this size cannot influence. Buyer power is high because the product is substitutable and imports set a reference price. The threat of substitutes is really the threat of imports, which is already being realised. Rivalry among domestic converters is intense precisely because the market is over-supplied relative to demand, which is what a sixty to seventy per cent utilisation rate means [S4, S5]. The one force that works in the company's favour is the barrier to entry created by capital: a calender line is expensive, which is why the fire was so damaging and why a new entrant is unlikely to build one to serve a market this contested.

Regulation cuts both ways. Trade remedies would help, and the minister has said the ministry will use the standards regime and anti-dumping where it can [S6]. Against that, the exchange's listing rule requires at least 15.0% of the shares to be held by the public below five per cent ownership, and the company does not meet it: the data pack puts the free float at 7.8% against that minimum [S0, S2, F29]. The rule is a structural overhang for a company whose public shareholders hold a small minority, and it affects the discount rate applied to a minority stake rather than this year's profit and loss [S0, S2, F29].

Indonesia's plastics industry sits at the end of a long petrochemical chain. Olefin crackers make ethylene and propylene, polymer plants turn those into polyethylene and polypropylene pellets, and converters like Asiaplast turn pellets into film, sheet and moulded articles. The country has been short of upstream cracker capacity for years, so converters import a large share of their resin, which ties domestic converting margins to a dollar-denominated input and to freight. Successive governments have tried to attract downstream investment to capture more of the chain locally, and the industry ministry routinely uses import measures when domestic utilisation falls. For a converter, the practical consequence is that the cost base is set internationally while the selling price is set locally, so the spread widens when the rupiah is strong or resin is cheap and narrows in the opposite case.

The reported history is a volume story told through a fire. Revenue fell from IDR526.8bn in FY2022A to IDR469.1bn, IDR399.7bn and IDR300.5bn, while the gross margin went from 20.7% to 24.9%, 17.2% and 11.8% [S2, S0]. The pattern is not a demand collapse followed by a price collapse; it is the loss of one machine's output in the fourth quarter of 2024, which removed high-margin flexible volume and left the fixed factory overhead of IDR59.8bn to be absorbed by fewer tonnes [S2, F11]. EBIT went from IDR66.5bn to IDR21.9bn and then turned negative, at IDR-6.2bn [S0]. Interest and other non-operating items turned that into a reported profit in FY2025 only because of the insurance claim [S2, F15].

We restate three lines that the data pack gets wrong, all from the audited statements. Depreciation and amortisation is the important one: the pack's depreciation line takes only the selling and general-and-administrative shares, roughly a fifth of the total, whereas the fixed-asset note reports depreciation and amortisation of IDR29.2bn for FY2025 and IDR28.0bn for FY2024, most of the charge sitting in cost of goods sold [S2, F1, F2]. The error matters twice: it understates historical EBITDA and it would have understated the capital intensity of the business. Second, finance costs were IDR1.7bn in FY2025 and IDR2.0bn in FY2024, not the smaller figure in the pack, which changes the implied interest rate on bank debt [S2, F3, F4]. Third, and most consequential for valuation, the pack's debt line carries only the short-term bank loans and omits the related-party loan described below [S2, F12].

That third point needs stating plainly. The balance sheet carries a loan from the ultimate controller to the subsidiary PT Tiga Berlian Electric of IDR41.1bn, which the related-party note describes as carrying no interest and no repayment term, and which is now about thirty-one per cent of total liabilities and unchanged from the prior year [S2, S7, F12, F13, F37]. The pack does not include it in debt, so the net cash position the pack reports is overstated by that amount. At 30 September 2026 the group had cash of IDR41.2bn and short-term bank loans of IDR26.0bn, a net cash position on the bank lines that becomes net debt once the loan is counted [S7, F34, F35, F37]. We deduct the loan once, as a bridge item in the valuation, so that the model's own debt line stays comparable with the pack while the equity value carries the liability [S0].

The forecast starts from the nine-month actual, not from an extrapolation. Revenue in the nine months to September was IDR247.3bn, so the fourth quarter has to deliver the balance for our FY2026E revenue of IDR347.9bn, which is a step up from the third quarter's run rate and is what a calender that has just restarted makes possible [S0, S7, F23, F30]. That is still about a third below the company's own target of IDR520.9bn for 2026, and far below its operating-profit target of IDR34.7bn [S2, F17, F18]. The operating target is not attainable: nine months delivered reported operating profit of IDR11.8bn of which IDR3.9bn was other income, and the fourth quarter would have to earn about three times the clean nine-month result to reach it [S7, S2, F18, F32, F38]. We do not use the company's targets because it missed its 2025 sales target by a wide margin, realising 78.8% of what it set out to do [S2, F19].

Growth then runs at 15.5%, 11.0%, 8.5% and 7.0% [S0]. On the FY2025 revenue per tonne and the productive base of about twenty-nine and a half thousand tonnes, that implies utilisation of about forty-three per cent in FY2026E, half in FY2027E, fifty-five per cent in FY2028E, sixty per cent in FY2029E and sixty-four per cent in FY2030E; on the full nameplate the FY2030E figure is fifty-four per cent [S0, S2, F5, F6, F26]. The base case therefore reaches the bottom of the sixty to seventy per cent band the association reports for the industry today, on the productive base, by the end of the explicit forecast, but does not reach it on the nameplate [S0, S4, S5]. Through FY2030E revenue of IDR517.9bn stays below the FY2022 peak of IDR526.8bn; the model crosses that peak in FY2031E and reaches IDR600.4bn by FY2035E [S0].

Margins are the judgement that matters most. We hold the gross margin at 20.2% at base input costs, which means at the FY2025A Brent price, and let the cost link apply the deck's oil path on top [S0, F10, F11]. Because the deck has Brent rising by about two fifths in FY2026E and falling back after, the reported margin is 16.8% in FY2026E and then 18.2%, 18.7% and 19.0% [S0]. The FY2026E figure is the nine-month actual: gross profit of IDR40.9bn on revenue of IDR247.3bn, a margin a shade under seventeen per cent, which the fourth quarter holds at the third quarter's rate [S7, F30, F31]. The bridge to the at-cost figure is explicit. FY2024 earned a gross margin of 17.2% at roughly half of the productive base, when the factory overhead of IDR59.8bn was spread over about fourteen and a half thousand tonnes; at the nineteen thousand tonnes implied by FY2030E revenue the same overhead is about three million rupiah a tonne instead of four, which is worth about three and a half points of margin and takes the FY2024 margin to about twenty and a half [S2, S0, F5, F11]. We hold twenty and a fraction rather than the full twenty and a half to allow for the PP and HIPS line and a less favourable mix [S2, F26].

The pass-through assumption is an explicit judgement, not a sourced fact. The annual report contains no statement that the company prices to cover costs, and we withdraw the earlier citation that said it did [S2]. We use eighty-five per cent because the nine-month gross margin was earned with Brent well above the FY2025 average, which is evidence that most of the cost move was recovered, and because a made-to-order converter with no customer above a tenth of revenue has room to reprice [S7, S2, F25]. The range is material: at full pass-through the FY2026E reported margin is about three and a half points higher, at the at-cost level, and at seventy per cent it is about three and a half points lower, around thirteen and a third per cent, because the unpassed share of the cost is what separates the at-cost margin from the reported one [S0, S2, F10]. At seventy per cent the margin does not return to the FY2025 trough, because volumes have recovered by then; it is the margin the plant earns if it recovers none of the resin increase [S0, S2].

The calibration from the trough year is the last bridge. FY2025A EBITDA margin was 7.6% and FY2026E is 13.2%, a gap of about five and a half points [S0]. It is bridged by the gross margin rising from 11.8% to 16.8%, worth about five points, by the SG&A ratio falling from the FY2025 level to 12.8% as the fixed establishment spreads over a larger revenue base, worth about one point, and by the D&A ratio falling from IDR29.2bn on FY2025 revenue to 9.2%, worth about half a point the other way [S0, S2, F11]. The volume and margin inputs to the bridge are the nine-month actuals, not our forecast, so the calibration rests on the filing [S7, F30, F31].

Operating cost is the second lever. Selling and administrative cost was IDR41.8bn in FY2025 against a collapsed revenue base; we model 12.8% of revenue in FY2026E and a decline to 10.5% by FY2030E as revenue grows against a largely fixed establishment and the loss-making electronics activity is shrunk [S0, S2, F9]. That gives an EBIT margin of 4.0% in FY2026E, 6.3% in FY2027E and 8.7% by FY2030E, against a FY2023 peak of 14.2% and a trough of -2.1% [S0].

Capital spending is front-loaded and then normalises. The nine-month accounts already carry capital expenditures of IDR42.6bn, of which IDR36.8bn is the replacement calender standing in assets under construction at 30 September, and cash advances for fixed assets of IDR46.7bn against an advance balance of IDR12.4bn that has risen from the year-end level [S7, F39, F40, F41, F42]. FY2026E therefore absorbs 14.6% of revenue, or IDR50.8bn: the nine-month cash outlay plus a fourth quarter of completion and maintenance spend. That falls to 7.7% and 6.4% thereafter, roughly in line with depreciation of 7.7% of revenue [S0, S2, F1]. That is the right shape for a company that has just bought its capacity: from FY2027E the cash flow is maintenance plus the working capital that growth requires, and there is no second expansion in the numbers because utilisation of the nameplate is still only 31.3% [S2, F7].

Cash conversion in the trough was strong, which is a genuine credit. Net profit minus operating cash flow, scaled by average assets, was negative in each of the last three years, meaning the company generated more cash than it reported as profit rather than capitalising costs into the balance sheet [S0]. That is unusual for a company in a volume downturn and it supports the view that the operating loss was an accounting consequence of a fire rather than a deterioration in the quality of the business [S0, S2]. The nine-month accounts show the same pattern: net profit of IDR7.5bn against a working-capital build that the coming year reverses as volumes settle [S7, F33].

Capital allocation is where the balance sheet becomes a governance question. The annual general meeting of 25 May 2026 approved a cash dividend of Rp44 a share for the financial year 2025 and the previous financial year together, with an ex-date of 8 June 2026 and payment on 26 June 2026 [S3, F21]. On the issued share count that is a payment of about IDR60.0bn, many times the FY2025 net profit, and it went out of a company whose controlling family holds the large majority of the shares [S3, S2, F21, F22]. Cash fell from IDR116.0bn at the end of FY2025 to IDR38.7bn at the end of our forecast year, and the distribution is why equity falls from IDR350.5bn to IDR302.7bn despite the profit [S0, F34]. We assume a 25.0% payout from FY2026E because the next dividend has to be funded from earnings, not from a stock of cash that has now been distributed [S0, S3].

The earnings-quality checklist leaves two flags. The first is the insurance claim: IDR8.7bn of other income in FY2025 turned an operating loss into a reported profit, and we strip it out entirely; the nine-month 2026 accounts carry IDR3.9bn of other income of which a large part is unexplained, and we strip that out too [S2, S7, F15, F16, F38]. The second is the related-party structure: the controller's loan is about thirty-one per cent of total liabilities, and key management compensation of IDR11.5bn was more than twice the FY2025 net profit [S2, S7, F12, F14, F37]. Against that, accruals are clean, there is no customer concentration, and the annual report states that there were no material legal cases or administrative sanctions in FY2025 [S2, F24, F25]. We do not find a revenue-recognition or capitalisation problem here; the flag is about who controls the cash, not about whether the numbers are real.

We value Asiaplast on a discounted cash flow, and the DCF is the target. A cyclical converter at a trough in its own volume cycle cannot be valued on a trailing earnings multiple, because the trailing figure reflects a plant that was not running, and VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL treats current-year multiples as the procyclical error it forbids [S0, S2]. The DCF lets a through-cycle Brent price and a normalised volume be stated explicitly, and it is the method the commodity-cyclical card prescribes for a name whose earnings are a function of utilisation and spread rather than of a franchise [S0]. We therefore carry the DCF at 100% of the target and the EV/EBITDA and P/E legs at zero [S0]. The multiples are not shown at all: the engine computes only methods that carry a weight, so a zero-weight leg produces no value and no table, and a multiple struck on the fire year would mislead a reader even as a floor.

The cost of capital is built from the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the Indonesian sovereign default spread of 1.6% to get a default-free rupiah rate, plus a re-levered beta times the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. The unlevered beta is 0.90, taken from the industry default, and it is re-levered at 0.95 using a debt-to-equity ratio of 7.7% [S0]. That ratio is one definition used once: gross bank debt over market capitalisation, which is the definition the engine uses to re-lever beta [S0]. It is not net debt to equity, and net debt is negative on the bank lines and positive only when the controller loan is included [S0, S2, F12]. The pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%, the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread of two percentage points; the company's own realised interest rate of seven point four per cent is used only for the interest expense on the bank lines in the profit and loss, not in the WACC [S0, S2, F3]. That produces a cost of equity of 12.2% and, at the statutory tax rate of 22.0%, a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9% [S0]. The IDR41.1bn controller loan is not treated as debt in the cost of capital: it pays no interest, it is deducted once at face in the bridge below, and that is why the gearing used to re-lever beta is 7.7% of bank debt only rather than a ratio that also carries the related-party claim [S2, F12, F13]. We have not added a size or governance premium; the illiquidity discount is applied separately at the end so that its effect is visible [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR333.9bn, of which 49.7% is terminal value, and a per-share value of Rp226 [S0]. Free cash flow is negative in FY2026E, at IDR-18.7bn, because the machine is being paid for and working capital is being rebuilt, turns positive in FY2027E at IDR20.2bn, and reaches IDR35.3bn by FY2030E as capital spending settles at the depreciation rate [S0]. The terminal value uses perpetual growth of 3.0%, which is the house terminal-growth cap for a rupiah name - a rounded midpoint of the deck's long-run rupiah inflation anchor and its CPI assumption - and well below nominal GDP growth, because this company's revenue has fallen over the last three years and a terminal assumption above inflation would be a growth claim it has not earned [S0, S2].

Two adjustments sit between the enterprise value and the equity value, and both are needed. The first is the controller loan of IDR41.1bn, deducted at face because the pack's debt line leaves it out and because we treat the loan as callable: it is repayable without a term and the bear case carries the cost of a call [S2, S7, F12, F13, F37]. If the loan were permanent capital the deduction would be smaller: discounting the zero-coupon claim at the bank rate over ten years values it at about half of face, which would add about fifteen rupiah a share, and we do not take that reading because the loan has no term and no covenant protecting a minority holder [S2, F13]. The second is the movement in net cash between the data pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet and the 30 September 2026 accounts, where cash of IDR41.2bn against bank loans of IDR26.0bn is about eleven billion rupiah better than the pack shows; the interim statements are the later evidence and the model uses them [S7, F34, F35].

The cross-checks are stated rather than blended. The house standard is a primary method plus two cross-checks. The engine computes only methods that carry a weight; the two the previous version blended were trailing multiples struck on the fire year, and the dividend-based alternatives rest on a payout the company has never committed to, so the DCF is the single engine method and we say so rather than dressing up a table that does not exist. Three checks bracket it without entering the target. The reverse DCF asks what growth the price requires: a 2.7% uplift to revenue growth in every forecast year, which is 18.2% in FY2027E against our 15.5% [S0]. The capital-backing check is book value: at Rp258 the shares stand at 1.2x FY2026E book, and our DCF of Rp226 is below the price, so the DCF implies a smaller premium to book than the market pays [S0]. The dividend-capacity check is the payout: Rp4 a share in FY2027E is 1.4% at the market price, which is the cash return the DCF has to beat [S0].

The gap to the market is now small, and the sensitivity shows why. At Rp258 the shares are 1.2x FY2026E book and 18.0x our FY2027E earnings [S0]. The operating grid, which varies revenue growth and the gross margin, has the base at its centre and reaches the price only in its upper region: the top cell, with growth and margin both well above our base, is about three-fifths above the centre, while the bottom cell is about two-fifths below it [S0]. The discount-rate grid is tighter: the price is reached only at a cost of capital a full point below ours, with terminal growth at or above our base [S0].

The commodity-cyclical contract is delivered here. The through-cycle price is the deck's long-run Brent of US$75.0/bbl, against a spot of US$97.1/bbl; the DCF carries the deck path from US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E down to US$78.0/bbl in FY2029E and the long-run price thereafter, so the NAV of Rp226 is struck on the through-cycle price rather than on spot [S0]. We do not publish a NAV at spot, and the reason is method rather than convenience: the deck spot is above the long-run price and above every explicit year of the path after FY2026E, so a DCF struck on spot would capitalise a war premium into perpetuity for a converter whose only exposure is about a tenth of cost of goods sold. Spot is cycle position, which the card treats as a timing input and never as value [S0, S2]. The cost-curve position is given as the trough-year EBITDA margin of 7.6% and factory overhead of IDR59.8bn on 10,970 MT of production, because a converter has no published cash-cost quartile [S2, F5, F11]. Dividend capacity is a 25.0% payout, which is Rp4 a share in FY2027E, a yield of 1.4% on the market price and a higher yield on our lower NAV [S0]. On the balance sheet at 30 September 2026, cash of IDR41.2bn against bank loans of IDR26.0bn is net cash on the bank lines; adding the controller loan of IDR41.1bn turns it into net debt of about one point one times the FY2025A trough EBITDA of IDR22.9bn, and about one point six times on the June balance sheet, which is comfortable against the FY2026E EBITDA of IDR45.8bn [S0, S2, S7, F34, F35, F37].

The target follows from the tree and the house discount, not from a blend. The probability-weighted value is Rp318 a share; the house illiquidity discount of 20% is applied because the stock trades about IDR106.7m a day against an equity value in the hundreds of billions, so an institution could not build or exit a position without moving the price, and that gives a target of Rp255 [S0]. Before the discount the tree implies about a quarter of upside, at the boundary between ADD and BUY; after it the target is -0.4% from the price, which is why the rating is HOLD and not an ADD [S0]. We state that arithmetic because it is the whole of the recommendation: the company is not overvalued, it is simply not cheap enough to compensate for the cost of owning a position this illiquid [S0].

The first risk is that the recovery is slower than we model, and it is the risk we are least able to dismiss. The replacement machine was already late once, the company's own account is that it will run only after mid-2026, and a commissioning delay of a further two quarters would push the volume recovery into FY2027E and leave a second year of under-absorbed overhead [S2, F23]. Our base case has revenue growing 15.8% in FY2026E and 15.5% in FY2027E, and the fourth quarter of FY2026E is already required to step up from the third quarter's run rate [S0, S7, F30]. A delay does not destroy value, because the capacity is still there, but it defers the cash flow that the valuation capitalises [S0].

The second is the import flood. The industry association's account is that domestic plants run at sixty to seventy per cent of capacity because imported plastic is dumped into the market, and the minister has promised to look at anti-dumping and standards measures without committing to any [S4, S5, S6]. If a remedy is imposed, the domestic price rises and utilisation improves across the industry, which is the main upside case [S5]. If none is imposed, Asiaplast has to win volume against an import price it cannot match, and the volume recovery we capitalise is the thing that fails [S4, S5].

The third is the resin spread. Raw materials are IDR186.0bn of cost of goods sold and the deck has Brent rising by about two fifths in FY2026E, so a company that cannot pass the increase through loses margin on every tonne [S2, F10, S0]. We assume an eighty-five per cent pass-through; at seventy per cent the FY2026E reported margin is about three and a half points lower, near thirteen and a third per cent, and the sensitivity grid shows the range [S0]. The saving grace is that the deck has Brent falling back from FY2027E, so this is a squeeze rather than a permanent change in the terms of trade [S0].

The fourth is the balance sheet and the family. The Rp44 dividend took most of the group's cash, the controller's loan of IDR41.1bn is repayable without a term, and the family owns the large majority of the shares [S2, S3, F12, F22]. We apply one characterisation throughout: the loan is callable. It is deducted at face in the bridge, and the bear case carries the cost of a call as a one-point addition to the cost of capital because the loan would have to be refinanced on the bank lines [S0, S2, F13]. The alternative reading, that the loan is permanent capital, would add about fifteen rupiah a share; we do not take it because nothing in the note protects a minority holder from a call [S2, F13].

The fifth is liquidity, index structure and dilution. The public holds 7.8% of the shares against the exchange's 15.0% minimum, and the stock trades a fraction of its equity value each day [S0, S2, F29]. Closing the gap by placing new shares at the current price would need about a hundred and fifteen million new shares if the whole gap were filled with new stock, an increase of about eight and a half per cent in the share count for about thirty billion rupiah of cash [S0, S2, F29]. On the company's own disclosure, which puts the public below five per cent at 12.7%, the gap is narrower and the dilution about a third as large [S2, F22]. At the market price that is close to value-neutral per share, because the cash raised is worth approximately what the new shares dilute, so we leave the forecast share count unchanged; a discounted placement or a rights issue is a real cost, and the bear narrative carries a discounted placement [S0, S2]. A placement would also be the cleanest route to the free float, which is why the rule and the dilution are discussed together [S2, F29].

The sixth is that the bull is not a forecast and should not be read as one. The tree is wide because the operating leverage is: a plant at a third of capacity has enormous incremental margin when volume returns, and the same leverage works against the holder when it does not [S0, S2, F7]. Our probabilities are base 50%, bear 25% and bull 25%. The bear is a genuine down cycle, with revenue growing eight points a year less than the base so that FY2029E and FY2030E fall, the at-cost gross margin down five and a half points so that the reported FY2026E margin of about eleven and a third per cent is below the FY2025 trough, working capital absorbing more cash, and the loan called and refinanced at a one-point higher cost of capital; it gives Rp44 [S0, S2, F7]. The bull has the calender at nameplate, an import measure, utilisation of about eighty-two per cent of the productive base by FY2030E, a reported margin that reaches but does not exceed the FY2023 peak, and a one-point lower cost of capital; it gives Rp726 [S0, S2, F11, F26]. The base gives Rp252 [S0].

The base rate is the reason the bull is weighted below the base case, and not at it. The desk's base-rate record puts commodity capex turnarounds at forty-two per cent with a large up move over three years, which is a higher hit rate than our twenty-five per cent bull [S0]. We do not match it because the base rate covers producers responding to a commodity price; this bull requires a specific policy decision on dumped imports that has not been announced, and a calender commissioning that is already late [S0, S2, S4, S5, F23]. If a remedy is imposed, the bull weight is too low; that is the piece of news we would pay for [S5, S6].

The signposts that would change our mind are specific. A fourth-quarter report showing the calender running and revenue above the third-quarter level would confirm the volume path, and we would raise the FY2027E revenue assumption [S2, S7, F23]. An imposed anti-dumping or safeguard measure would lift the whole industry's price and would justify the bull case, so a ministerial announcement is the single most valuable piece of news this name can receive [S5, S6]. A decision to repay the controller's loan without new bank debt would remove the balance-sheet overhang and the call risk [S2, F13]. And the terms of any free-float placement would settle the dilution question: a placement at or above the market price is close to neutral, a deep discount is not [S0, S2, F29].

Control is concentrated and the structure is layered. PT Maco Amangraha holds the controlling block, the ultimate beneficiary is Alexander Agung Pranoto, who is also President Commissioner, and the family chain runs through his wife and sons, while the public holding below five per cent is 12.7% [S2, F22]. The data pack's free float of 7.8% is lower than the 12.7% the company discloses for holders below five per cent, the difference turning on which family and affiliate stakes each definition excludes; on either measure the company is short of the minimum, widely on the registry measure and narrowly on its own [S0, S2, F22, F29]. There is no independent block that could check a related-party decision, and the board's composition follows from the ownership [S2, F22].

The related-party loan is the substantive governance issue. A loan of IDR41.1bn from the ultimate controller to a subsidiary, carrying no interest and no repayment term, is not intrinsically abusive; it is cheaper funding than the bank lines and it has been stable across three balance-sheet dates [S2, S7, F12, F13, F37]. But it is about thirty-one per cent of total liabilities, it is invisible in the data pack's debt line, and it gives the controller a claim on the company that ranks alongside the banks while paying nothing [S2, S7, F12, F37]. If the family ever needs liquidity, that claim can be called, and the dividend record shows a willingness to move large amounts of cash out of the company: the FY2025 payment of Rp44 a share covered two financial years at once and exceeded the year's net profit many times over [S3, F21].

The dividend is the clearest signal of how minority holders are treated. The company paid a small dividend for FY2023, nothing for FY2024, and then a large catch-up in June 2026; equity falls from IDR350.5bn at the end of FY2025 to IDR302.7bn at the end of our forecast year because the distributions take out more than the profit adds [S3, F21, S0]. Most of that money went to the controlling family [S2, F22]. There is no stated ratio policy: the annual report says only that any dividend will be decided at the annual meeting after considering working capital, capital spending, prospects and financial condition [S2]. A minority holder should therefore treat the dividend as a family decision, not as a commitment, and should not capitalise the FY2025 payment as a recurring yield [S2, S3, F21].

Capital allocation also includes an authorisation that has not been used. The extraordinary meeting of 13 June 2025 approved a buyback of up to 10.0% of paid-up capital, with a cost cap of about seventy-two billion rupiah, for the period from June to the end of December 2025, and the company states that it had not bought any shares as of 31 December 2025 [S2, F28]. The window has therefore closed, the annual report says a buyback only makes sense when the market price is well below intrinsic value, and it notes that the free-float rule constrains one because the public already holds too little [S2, F28, F29]. We do not treat the authorisation as support for the price; we treat it as evidence that management is aware of the float problem and has not yet acted on it [S2, F28, F29].

Management pay is out of proportion to the business. Total compensation of the commissioners and directors was IDR11.5bn in FY2025 against a net profit of IDR5.6bn, and it was higher the year before, when the operating result was still positive [S2, F14]. That is a small absolute number but a large fraction of the earnings a minority holder owns, and it is the kind of item that never falls when volumes do [S2, F14]. The annual report states that there were no material legal cases or administrative sanctions involving the company or its boards in FY2025, and we rely on that disclosure and on nothing further [S2, F24].

On ESG the exposures are the industry's rather than the company's own. Plastics converting is energy-intensive and its product sits at the centre of the packaging-waste debate, and the company publishes sustainability disclosure alongside the annual report [S2]. We have not found a disclosed environmental liability, and nothing in the accounts suggests a remediation provision [S2]. The more relevant social and governance issue for a minority holder is the free float: the exchange's minimum of 15.0% is a structural requirement the company does not currently meet, and how it is addressed, whether by a placement, a share split or a continued exemption, will affect the shareholder register and the index treatment over the next few years [S0, S2, F29].

Indonesian listed companies have historically been allowed to list with a small public float, and a large share of the small-cap universe is controlled by families or conglomerates. The exchange has been tightening the minimum free-float requirement, with a phased timetable, in an effort to improve liquidity and to satisfy index providers who require a minimum float for inclusion. Companies that cannot meet the threshold have to place shares, do a rights issue, or accept exclusion from benchmarks. For a minority investor the practical consequences are a persistent liquidity discount, index-driven selling when a review is announced, and a governance discount that reflects the controlling shareholder's ability to direct related-party transactions. None of this is unique to any one company; it is the structural backdrop against which small Indonesian caps have to be valued.

The near-term disclosure has already happened: the third-quarter accounts were published with the 30 September 2026 interim report, and they show the calender's first contribution, with revenue of IDR247.3bn and a gross margin a shade under seventeen per cent for the nine months [S7, F30, F31]. The next scheduled catalyst is the FY2026 results, the first set of accounts to include the restarted calender, followed by the annual general meeting that will set the FY2026 dividend [S2, S3]. The industry ministry's decision on trade remedies remains the largest potential positive, and the free-float deadline is the largest structural negative [S5, S6, S2, F29].

Between reports we monitor four numbers: plastics production against the 35,000 MT nameplate, the gross margin against the resin path in the deck, the level of the controller loan and whether it is serviced or repaid, and the free-float position against the exchange's minimum [S2, S0, F6, F12, F29]. A move in either of the first two changes the valuation; a move in either of the last two changes the discount applied to it [S0]. We also watch the terms of any placement, because a placement at the market price is close to value-neutral and a discounted one is not [S0, S2, F29].
